meta.name: Hinglish ASR Test Set — Part 1
meta.author: Samyak
meta.purpose: Evaluation input corpus for faster-whisper (large-v3, language=hi) on conversational Hinglish. Used to produce real p50/p95 ASR latency measurements (see docs/findings/perf-1-latency-budget.md).

recording_spec.speaker: single human voice
recording_spec.note: These are transcription inputs, not TTS-generated clips. Each case must be recorded by a human speaker.

notes: Do NOT fabricate ASR output. The expected_script field describes anticipated script behaviour from the spike (asr-hinglish.md), not a measured result.
Cases are designed to cover the categories identified in docs/spikes/asr-hinglish.md.
Part 1 covers short-to-medium utterances (2-8 s). Long utterances and multi-turn interaction are deferred to Part 2.
The duration_budget_s field is a recording target, not a hard limit.

cases.label: Pure Hindi — greeting
cases.what_it_checks: Baseline: pure Hindi greeting. Establishes that the pipeline writes Devanagari for Hindi-only speech without any code-switching artefacts.
cases.notes: Should be the easiest case. Failure here is a hard blocker.

cases.label: Pure Hindi — instruction with time
cases.text: कल सुबह मुझे आठ बजे याद दिला देना।
cases.romanized: Kal subah mujhe aath baje yaad dila dena.
cases.what_it_checks: Pure Hindi sentence with a time reference. Verifies correct Devanagari rendering of a common conversational request without any English words present.
cases.notes: Close to the committed initial_prompt from asr-hinglish.md. Should transcribe cleanly.

cases.label: Pure English — everyday request
cases.text: Can you book me a table for two at eight tonight?
cases.what_it_checks: Forces language=hi on clean English speech. The spike (section 4) showed large-v3 leaves clean English intact when using the real model. Confirms this holds for a human speaker, not TTS.
cases.notes: Regression guard: if this fails, forcing language=hi is broken for English-only users. This exact sentence appeared in the spike.

cases.label: Pure English — longer technical sentence
cases.text: The quarterly report is due on Friday, please send me your numbers by Wednesday afternoon.
cases.what_it_checks: Longer English utterance under language=hi. The spike used this sentence (cut mid-word) to expose the Devanagari-repetition-loop failure on partial decodes. Recorded in full, the whole-utterance decode should be safe.
cases.notes: Spike section 4b showed loops occur only on cut-off audio. Full recording expected to produce correct Latin output.

cases.label: Light mix — English noun embedded in Hindi sentence
cases.text: मुझे कल एक meeting attend करनी है।
cases.romanized: Mujhe kal ek meeting attend karni hai.
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for Hindi words; Latin for meeting and attend
cases.what_it_checks: Most common real-world Hinglish pattern: a Hindi sentence with one or two borrowed English nouns. Checks that the code-switch is preserved (Latin for English words) and not collapsed into all-Devanagari.
cases.notes: The spike showed this type works on large-v3 with language=hi. Priority case.

cases.label: Light mix — English verb phrase embedded in Hindi
cases.text: क्या तुम मेरे लिए यह file upload कर सकते हो?
cases.romanized: Kya tum mere liye yeh file upload kar sakte ho?
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for Hindi words; Latin for file and upload
cases.what_it_checks: English technical verb + noun pair inside a Hindi question. Tests whether the model correctly code-switches on common tech vocabulary used in Indian workplace conversation.
cases.notes: A common conversational pattern in Indian workplaces.

cases.label: Light mix — English discourse marker at sentence start
cases.text: Actually, mujhe nahi lagta ki yeh theek rahega.
cases.romanized: Actually, mujhe nahi lagta ki yeh theek rahega.
cases.expected_script: Latin for Actually; Devanagari for the rest
cases.what_it_checks: English discourse marker at the start of an otherwise Hindi sentence. Very common in spoken Hinglish. Tests sentence-initial code-switch, which is a different pattern from noun/verb borrowing mid-sentence.
cases.notes: Discourse markers such as actually, basically, and I mean are a distinct linguistic pattern from borrowing content words.

cases.label: Heavy mix — spike sample B sentence (exact reuse)
cases.text: जितना ज़्यादा clear करोगे, उतना ज़्यादा अच्छे से ASI respond करेगा।
cases.romanized: Jitna zyada clear karoge, utna zyada achhe se ASI respond karega.
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for Hindi words; Latin for clear, ASI, respond
cases.what_it_checks: This is the exact sample used in the ASR spike (asr-hinglish.md sample B, forced-hi row). Using the identical sentence lets us compare real human recording results directly against the spike results from a TTS clip.
cases.notes: Spike reference output: जितना ज्यादा clear कोईंगे उसमें शायद इतना ज्यादा अच्छे से ASI respond कोईगा. Deviations between human recording and TTS clip are expected and informative.

cases.label: Heavy mix — dense alternation with English fillers
cases.text: Matlab, basically yeh kaam already ho gaya hai, but confirmation nahi aayi abhi tak.
cases.romanized: Matlab, basically yeh kaam already ho gaya hai, but confirmation nahi aayi abhi tak.
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for matlab, kaam, nahi, abhi tak; Latin for basically, already, but, confirmation
cases.what_it_checks: Dense mixing: mid-sentence alternation between Hindi and English at roughly equal density. Tests the model's handling of rapid script switches within a single short sentence.
cases.notes: Near-equal language density. More script-switching failures expected here than in light-mix cases.

cases.label: Heavy mix — Vaani project sentence (used in Day 11 measurement)
cases.text: Namaste, aaj hum real-time voice conversation ke baare mein baat karenge.
cases.romanized: Namaste, aaj hum real-time voice conversation ke baare mein baat karenge.
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for Hindi words; Latin for real-time, voice, conversation
cases.what_it_checks: The sentence used in Piper TTS clips and in the Day 11 measure_turn.py end-to-end run (perf-1-latency-budget.md). Including the same sentence recorded by a human speaker allows comparison: TTS clip ASR decode time of 1188 ms vs human voice decode time.
cases.notes: The single most referenced Hinglish sentence in the project. Must be included.

cases.label: Numbers and dates — Hindi number-words with English month name
cases.text: मीटिंग पाँच अक्तूबर को है, दोपहर तीन बजे।
cases.romanized: Meeting paanch October ko hai, dopahar teen baje.
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for Hindi words; Latin for Meeting and October may vary
cases.what_it_checks: Dates and times in spoken Hinglish frequently mix Hindi number-words with English month names. Tests numeric and date word handling which is relevant to scheduling assistant queries.
cases.notes: ASR output for month names and numbers may be inconsistent across runs. Record the exact output each time.

cases.label: Numbers and dates — price with Hindi number-words
cases.text: Iski price approximately paanch sau rupaye hai.
cases.romanized: Iski price approximately paanch sau rupaye hai.
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for paanch sau rupaye; Latin for price, approximately
cases.what_it_checks: Currency and quantity phrases common in shopping or travel queries. Tests that Hindi numeral words are written in Devanagari and English modifiers in Latin.

cases.label: Question — English opener then Hindi clarification
cases.text: Sorry, can you please repeat that? Mujhe samajh nahi aaya.
cases.romanized: Sorry, can you please repeat that? Mujhe samajh nahi aaya.
cases.expected_script: Latin for the English question; Devanagari for the Hindi follow-on
cases.what_it_checks: Natural user clarification pattern: English opener, Hindi explanation. Tests sentence-boundary code-switching. Also tests whether a question mark mid-utterance causes the pipeline to split into two transcripts prematurely.
cases.notes: The transcript pipeline may split this into two turns depending on VAD and endpointing. Record as one continuous utterance without a long pause between the two halves.

cases.label: Question — Hindi WH-question with embedded English nouns
cases.expected_script: Devanagari for Aapka, kya, hai; Latin for office, address
cases.what_it_checks: Short question with embedded English nouns. Common in voice assistant usage. Tests that the model does not hallucinate or collapse short questions when language=hi is forced.
cases.notes: Short utterances under 3 s are more vulnerable to VAD filter edge cases. Record with clear speech onset and a clean silence after the final word.
